utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today, we are Tuesday. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us. We have started our hearing somewhat late because two of my colleagues were involved in another trial this morning, and we could therefore not start at a quarter to. We started at a quarter to 3.00 today and not at a quarter past 2.00. Tomorrow, we will also start at a quarter to 3.00. On Thursday, we shall sit at 9.00 in the morning, since this courtroom will be available. We shall therefore sit on Thursday morning in this courtroom. This will be either in Courtroom I or in Courtroom II on Thursday. The next witness is going to come into the courtroom. From what I understand, there are no protective measures. The Prosecution has two hours, Mr. Seselj has two hours. Mr. Seselj, I believe you would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, I have to inform you that my legal associates calculated the time that was spent during the cross-examination of the last witness, and they came to the conclusion that you took away 35 minutes of my time. One hour and 25 minutes is the time that I took up, effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall check this. I wasn't under that impression, but maybe there's been a mistake. We shall have a close look at this. Registrar, can we have the countdown of last week's hearing, please, to see whether or not we have taken some of Mr. Seselj's time, i.e., 25 [as interpreted] minutes. Mr. Seselj, we shall keep you informed. As you know, our computer system enables us to check the time each party has had. On the basis of these calculations, the Registrar tells us how much time each have had. I usually put the question to the Registrar during the hearing to see how much time each party has had and how much time is left. The Registrar tells me there are 30 minutes left, 40 minutes left, 5 minutes left, on a little Post-It. This is how I'm able to keep track of this. There might have been a mistake, I don't know, but this is how we proceed. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom now, please, unless Mr. Mundis would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, to Dr. Seselj, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. I do have two points that I would like to raise at this point, if I may, Your Honours. Before I do that, I would like to take this opportunity to introduce another member of our trial team to the Chamber. Mr. Francesco Rindi is with us today, who's one of the legal officers on this case. The first issue I'd like to raise, Your Honours, concerns a confidential motion that was filed last week. I believe we can deal with this in open session. On the 6th of June, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting to order a variation in protective measures concerning Witness VS-1057. During a proofing session yesterday, that witness informed the Prosecution that he had changed his mind and that he is now prepared to testify in open public session before the Tribunal, without any protective measures. In view of this position taken by the witness, as informed to us late yesterday afternoon, the Prosecution withdraws its motion for protective measures concerning this witness that was filed on the 6th of June, 2008. At the same time, we would invite the Trial Chamber, if need be, to explore this issue with the witness immediately prior to his testimony to ascertain if, in fact, that is still the position that he takes. But, again, he informed us late yesterday that he does not want the protective measures set forth in that motion and is prepared to testify in open session without any protective measures. So we do withdraw that motion, but again we would invite the Trial Chamber, if the Chamber deems it important or necessary, to perhaps raise the issue with the witness directly, immediately before his testimony, which we expect to commence late in the day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly - Mr. Seselj would like to respond - the Witness 1057 has told you that he does not wish to have protective measures anymore. You are saying that the Trial Chamber should record his request. In other words, before asking the witness to take the solemn declaration, we will have the blinds dropped and, in private session, say to the witness, "You did ask to have protective measures. You advised the Prosecution of the fact that you do not wish to have protective measures anymore. Can you confirm this?" The witness will then say either "yes" or "no," and if he says he no longer wants protective measures, then we shall move into open session. Is that the subject of your request?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Only to the extent, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber thinks that that would be an important step to take, in light of the fact that the witness had requested this and then subsequently changed his mind. Perhaps out of an abundance of caution, the Chamber might adopt that approach and use the procedure that the Presiding Judge has just specified. We are entirely in the Trial Chamber's hands in that respect. We leave it up to you to make a decision amongst yourselves as to whether or not you think that would be a prudent course of action, in light of these developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I was getting ready to challenge the request of the Prosecutor for protective measures for this witness, and now it seems that the Prosecutor surprised me pleasantly by giving up on his own request. However, I want to take this opportunity to draw your attention to something else. So far, decisions were reached with great ease to grant protective measures to protect Prosecution witnesses. So far, there have been 24 witnesses here, many with protective measures, and I am absolutely convinced that not in a single case were there any reasons whatsoever for protective measures, not in a single case. That is something that has become current practice in this Tribunal. It happens in other trials and cases as well. It is sufficient for a witness to express that kind of wish, and protective measures are granted straight away. You had here high-level functionaries of the regime, I'd like to put it that way, but you had high-level military officials with protective measures, you had notorious criminals with protective measures, you had people who agreed to testify in court because they were granted asylum in a Western country, and means for a proper life, and so on. Not a single witness who comes from the area of Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia is under any threat from me, or my associates, or my ideological followers and political supporters, absolutely no one is threatened. Protective measures are always asked for with something else in mind. It is primarily protection from the shame of false testimony. They are exclusively protection from shame against false testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are again talking about false testimonies. You know that the Trial Chamber has asked you not to say this, because this does have consequences. The Trial Chamber is currently working on this issue, to the effect that we have not handed down our decision yet. We are currently putting the finishing touches on our decision. Every time the words "false testimony" or "false witnesses" come up on the screen, we shall redact these terms. I believe Mr. Mundis was on his feet to object to this. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President, the Prosecution objects to any and all characterizations of false testimony and false witnesses, but I also rise to my feet simply to make the point that it is, in our respectful views, inappropriate for Mr. Seselj to be speaking globally about protective measures for witnesses. As this Chamber knows, protective measures are issued on a case-by-case basis, and if necessary and if the Chamber feels that protective measures are necessary for every single witness in this case, then so be it. Those decisions are taken on a case-by-case, witness-by-witness basis, on the basis of information made available by the witness. And so it really is simply not a productive use of our time to have a speech about the general nature of protective measures or the fact that a large number of witnesses have protective measures. This is simply something that is not a productive use of the time that's available to us, and I would respectfully ask that we move on to more important topics that need to be addressed today and to get the witness into the box so that Your Honours can hear the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj. Two things, Mr. Seselj. You said a while ago that 24 witnesses had been granted protective measures. I don't know, you might be wrong --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You might be right, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but a number of witnesses who have come to testify, well, a lot of these witnesses have testified without protective measures. I even have the feeling that the majority of witnesses have testified without protective measures. I don't have any clear-cut figures to give you, but that is the feeling I have. The second point: As far as protective measures are concerned, protective measures are part of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In some countries like mine, these do not exist, with the exception of minors who come to testify in closed session. In a number of countries, protective measures have been established, including in your own country, where there are trials ongoing and people who benefit from protective measures. Protective measures are asked by the witness. The Trial Chamber only grants the protective measures if the potential risks at stake are valid. We don't grant protective measures to all and every one haphazardly. This is why I would like you to turn to the decision taken by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecutor had filed a consolidated motion. We granted the Prosecution's motion as regards a number of witnesses and disagreed as regards a number of other witnesses. In addition, in our decision we had stated that all of this could be reassessed, and in the course of these reassessments, these things happen. For instance, a witness who had been granted protective measures decided not to testify with protective measures. When a witness comes, we can put the question to the witness, and I would like to say this again, because one is under the impression sometimes that protective measures are given to all and everyone. Protective measures are granted, and in some cases the Trial Chamber has no latitude, because these protective measures have been granted by another Trial Chamber. In the Milosevic trial, for instance, the witnesses that came to testify were granted protective measures. We need to abide by that. There are some witnesses who come to testify who've already testified in other trials, who have been granted protective measures, and we have no latitude to change this. I think this has to be quite clear. This Trial Chamber can do nothing as far as those witnesses are concerned. However, we have full discretion to decide what the status of witnesses who have not testified in other trials is to be. When a witness asks to be granted protective measures, we listen, after having heard you. This is how it works, and you know this as well as we do. So far, we have not run into major difficulties, and this is why I can put the question to the witness every time, ask the witness whether he or she has testified in another trial, and sometimes we discover that those witnesses have been granted protective measures in domestic courts, and this is something we know nothing about. This happened last time, since like you, you discovered this. So we're extremely careful with this. As a rule, the witnesses testify in open session, unless of course protective measures are granted to some witnesses and victims, which is something all and everyone understands in this courtroom. Now, we have to move on because we have a witness who is going to come to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this gives rise to a new problem, the problem of translation that we had earlier on. I never said that 24 witnesses had protective measures. Secondly, while Serbia was a civilised country, which was until a short while ago, like France, France did not have protective measures for witnesses, except for rape victims and serious victims like that.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: In the spirit of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY, protective measures are an exception. They are possible, but very, very seldom. However, as they are applied here, they have become a rule. In my case, there are more witnesses with protective measures than those that will testify without protective measures. We had witnesses who gave up on that here in the courtroom, like Goran Stoparic and some others. Perhaps we will have more of them. But at the outset, we had more protected witnesses than those who testify as one should, in public. I'm just asking for something that is an exception, according to the Rules should be applied here in exceptional cases only. Of course, there can be victims of sex crimes here, too, and that kind of person should testify in closed session. Perhaps a minor may come to testify, but that is hard to envisage, since the war happened a long time ago. Perhaps even something like that will be something that the Prosecution will come up with. Perhaps somebody who was planned to be born during the war will come as a witness some day and the Prosecutor will call them with protective measures. But there is no reason for this. The Prosecution is talking about some facts that I'm not aware of, that witnesses are being threatened, intimidated and so on. You know what? The hostile attitude of the Serbian public towards The Hague Tribunal was created by the Tribunal itself, and that was additionally supported by Carla Del Ponte in her book, and then that woman of hers, what was her name, Hartman, and she published a book, and then Jeffrey Nice, who is giving interviews left, right and center. As soon as somebody leaves the Tribunal, they start throwing sticks and stones at the Tribunal. The hostile attitude of the Serbian public toward the Tribunal is the result of the cumulative effect of different factors, and it cannot be a reason for closing sessions here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'll give the floor to Mr. Mundis in a minute, but contrary to what you're saying, Mr. Seselj, out of 24 witnesses who testified, 12 testified without any protective measures. That's 50 per cent. The figures speak for themselves. You can ask your associates to check that. Twenty-four people came here to testify, and twelve testified without any protective measures whatsoever. Out of the 12 others that were granted protective measures, I believe that most of them had been granted protective measures by the other Trial Chambers, and therefore my fellow Judges and myself had no latitude to do anything. This is how things stand. I believe that things must be said, because when hearing you, somebody from the outside could say, "Well, he's right, after all." Well, you are right to a certain extent. 50 per cent of the witnesses were granted protective measures, but out of these 50 per cent, this Trial Chamber could do nothing about it because these protective measures had been granted by other Trial Chambers. However, I have the number of witnesses for which protective measures were granted by this Trial Chamber for reasons that were mentioned at length. The Trial Chamber is extremely sensitive when it comes to this problem, and we do our utmost to make sure that we don't run into lengthy discussions on this issue. This is what I had to say. Now, let's bring the witness into the courtroom, please. Could the usher, please, bring the witness in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check first that you hear the translation of what I'm saying in your own language. If so, please tell me. Could you please, sir, give us your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perica Koblar, 6th of August, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job at the moment, and if so, what job do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am unemployed, but I work as a private person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What activity do you work in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an instructor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified in a tribunal, be it domestic or international on what happened in the former Yugoslavia, or is it the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not officially before a court, but in Sarajevo, before a unit and under investigation when I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you were captured, you testified for the investigation; is that it? You were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. Thank you. Witness, before giving the floor to the Prosecutor, who's going to put some questions to you, let me tell you exactly what is going to happen. You will be asked questions by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor may also show you some documents. So just answer the questions. If you don't understand the meaning of the question, you can ask the person putting the question to reformulate that question. Please try to be specific in your answers. At the end of the questions put to you by the Prosecutor, the accused, Mr. Seselj, who is on your left, will also be asking questions to you. He will be given the same amount of time for questions as the Prosecutor had. The three Judges on the Bench can also ask questions at any time, and I'm sure that we will do so at one moment or another. Every hour and a half, we break for 20 minutes so you can rest. We might not finish your testimony today. Therefore, we will ask you to come back tomorrow at quarter to 3.00, but normally we should finish your testimony tomorrow. Now, you are now the witness of justice, and therefore you should not have any contact whatsoever with the OTP. You are not supposed to contact the person you saw recently for the proofing session. This is what I had to tell you. There are a couple of other things I need to tell you. If at any point in time you don't feel very well, feel uneasy, just raise your hand and ask for a break and for the hearing to be adjourned for a moment. If you also want to ask a question to the Bench, you can do so, you can put questions to us. This is all I had to say, and I will now give the floor to the Prosecutor for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Koblar. As you know, your testimony is in open session. Therefore, if at any time you mention names or a place that you do not wish to be broadcast to the public, please warn the Judge, explaining the reason why you do not want this to happen, and the Judge will decide whether we should continue in closed session or not. Let's start with some basic information on your personal and professional background. When were you born?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The 6th of August, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Ivangrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How long did you live there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Only for a few years.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you move to some other town?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: To Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The 1960s. I don't know exactly, 1965, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How long did you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I still live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Are you married; do you have children?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Divorced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your education.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: A technical vocational school, a secondary school for catering. Then I got a degree in political science at the university, and now I'm doing a post-graduate course at the Faculty of Political Sciences at the university there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I think this is a personal question. I never asked anyone what their ethnicity or religion were. I will tell you that before, I used to be a Yugoslav, and now I'm a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you undergo the compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes, in 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was your speciality?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Radio operator at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did the conflict in Sarajevo start?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Well, as soon as the first barricades were set up after the referendum concerning the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you get involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: On the 2nd of March, I returned from Trebevic, and I clashed with the people who were at the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you join the reserve forces of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: That was the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Novo Sarajevo, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did you join this Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The same day that I reported to MUP that I had been attacked and beaten up at that barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we have the document bearing the 65 ter number 7234 displayed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes. That is my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: It is the accreditation of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Novo Sarajevo, and it has the number 000087.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who released it to you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you be more specific on the date when did you join the TO?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Well, a couple of days after the 2nd of March, after the end of the referendum, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P458.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you involved in any combat operations in Sarajevo, and when?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Until the direct attack took place on the 2nd of May, there were no military operations in that part of the town covered by this particular unit of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to approach the microphones and speak up, please. Thank you. We're having trouble hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When you say "2nd of May," which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Have you ever been wounded?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Officially, twice, and two more times, light wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where and when were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The first time was at Pero Kosoric Square when I was on duty; and the second time, at the beginning of December, 1992 -- or rather that was the first time, and the second time at the end of April, when I was running over the runway of the airport and leaving Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Regarding the first time that you were wounded, did you have to undergo any medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: For how long and where did you receive this treatment?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: At the military hospital in Sarajevo, right up until I think it was the 26th of April, when I left Sarajevo at Bjelasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What did you do once you recovered?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: When I was running across the runway, I was wounded in my right leg again, and I was treated at Igman of that wound, and continued treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: But when did it happen -- this happen, the second injury?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: There's a document about it, but I think it was the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please have the document bearing 65 ter number 7236 displayed on the screen. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, can you comment on this document? What does it show?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The date of the wounding. It says down there: "While in a combat assignment at Heroj Square." However, in this document, it doesn't say that I was wounded on the 26th on the runway, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who released this document?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The 101st Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that there is a lot of interference and noise in the courtroom and they find it very difficult to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P459.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. On the document, it says the Command of the Army of Yugoslavia. What does that mean, "VJ"? So could the Prosecutor explain to us what that abbreviation "VJ" means. As far as I know, it is Vojska Jugoslavija or Army of Yugoslavia, or perhaps it means something else and I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, can you explain us what does it mean, "Command of the VJ"?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The military unit 63 -- it's a military unit, short for "military unit," and then the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So what does it mean in B/C/S, exactly?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Vojna Jedinica, meaning military unit, and then the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Koblar.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: 6359 is the number. It's the military unit of Vojna Jedinica of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object again. It doesn't say that it's the BH Army anywhere here. You can't see that from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, Mr. Seselj made a comment and I made myself the same comment, you know. What does "VJ" mean. You said that it's "Vojna Jedinica," that's what it means in your own language. Military unit 6359, that must be the 101 Motorised Brigade. I assume it is. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this document, it says "Military unit," but it doesn't say "BH" because the document was issued in 1999 and it was the Army of the Federation. But that's not on the document, either. But the document is an original one, and you can find it in the archive of the 101st Motorised Brigade of the BH Army of the time, as well as in the 1st Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In 1999, you requested a certificate, mentioning that you had been injured, and the Army of the Federation delivered this certificate. I would like to tell Mr. Seselj, but I'm sure he noticed it because he notices everything, that there is a stamp next to the name of the person signing. The photocopy is not clear, but we do see the coat of arms of the Federation. So this is an official document. Notably, and this is something I would like to tell to Mr. Seselj, but I'm sure he noticed it also, but there is a number. There is a number, 312524130303183/99, so this document can be found -- the original can be found in the archives of the army of today's Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, from the stamp -- or, rather, on the stamp all we can see is the coat of arms of the old medieval dynasty Kotromanic, and that's a Serb coat of arms which was used by Izetbegovic's regime when it represented itself as being the supreme power in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was then used -- whether it was used in the Federation, I don't know. We can't see that anywhere here. Anyway, this is an old medieval crest of the Serbian Kingdom of Bosnia, whose king was crowned in Mileseva at St. Sava's grave, and it doesn't say anywhere that it has anything to do with Izetbegovic's regime; neither does it say that this is the Bosnia Federation. We have nothing on this document, so we have to believe the witness at his word that he's wounded, and I wouldn't doubt that at all. I wouldn't cross-examine him about that; I do believe that he was wounded. But this document shows nothing at all. It has no probative value whatsoever because it hasn't got any of the basic markings that it should have, that an authentic document should have on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In a word, Mr. Seselj, are you challenging the reality of this document or are you saying that this person was indeed wounded, but you are raising doubts as to the persons who actually drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on this document we have none of the official markings. We can't see which state issued it. We cannot see a stamp, either. So there is no basic data which such a document would require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Koblar, could you give us some information? Where did you get this document, first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just make a short comment? Judging by everything, the accused is trying to say I was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. This is an official document of the BH Army which can be found even in the present joint Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the 101st Motorised Brigade of the BH Army and also in the documents of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, as far as the stamp is concerned, this is the stamp of medieval Bosnia, as a state, and not a Serb state, not that of a Serb state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did you obtain this document? You must have gone to an office. Where did you go to get this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my unit of the 101st Motorised Brigade, the Viktor Bubanj barracks or Ramiz Salcin which is where the BH Court is now located. THE COURT: Very well. So you went over there. You gave your name. They checked on their lists whether you had been a soldier in the 101st Motorised Brigade. Somebody must have filled the document and stamped it and then handed it over to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I didn't have to prove anything, because the military booklet of BH members exists. I didn't have to prove anything, just asked for a document to be issued so that I could solve some of my life's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A small mystery. In 1999, there was the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, since this is after the Dayton Agreements and the Washington Agreements. There is a high representative over there. Why is it that such a stamp was affixed, rather than the stamp for the Armed Forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? You and Mr. Seselj do say that this is a stamp with a reference to the Middle Ages. Why is it that there is no official stamp of the Federation on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this document, you had the stamp which was used as the emblem of the BH Army, which had still not been replaced at that time with a new stamp. That was the stamp that was used.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the stamp of the Federation has, in one portion, has the old Bosnian medieval coat of arms and, in part, the Croatian coat of arms, so that cannot be a stamp of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I think it is a matter of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, you're quite right, but irrespective of this procedural matter, theoretically they should have stamped it with the stamp of the Federation. Why is another stamp used in this instance? Before you were interrupted, I think it was because they didn't have the new stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember exactly when the joint flag and emblems of the Federation was introduced. Perhaps during that period, because unless I'm mistaken, it was during that time that the coat of arms of the cantons were introduced and of the Federation, too. However, this document, and we have -- the original of this document exists and you can find it to see what it looks like, it can be found in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we'll stop there, as far as that particular question is concerned. Please proceed, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Koblar, you were wounded the first time on the 7th December, 1992. When did you rejoin your unit after you recovered from this injury?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: We went straight away to Bjelasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Well, precisely that same day or the previous day, because I had to run across the runway. There wasn't a tunnel there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: The same day, or the previous day, or what?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Before being wounded, before I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: The first time or the second time?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The second time, on the 26th of April, because I was wounded on the runway on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Now it's clear. So you rejoined your unit, and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: From my unit, some 50 men went to Bjelasnica for a preparation of sorts, and not to say for a bit of a rest too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What did you do there, and how long do you stay there in Bjelasnica?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Up until the beginning of July, when the military operations of the Army of Republika Srpska started and the Chetnik units at Bjelasnica and the surrounding parts of Sarajevo, Rogoj, Igman, Bjelasnica, that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were saying something which might be unimportant, as far as you're concerned, but we feel that this is highly important. You have said that the military operations of Republika Srpska and of the Chetnik units. What are these Chetnik units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those units who were not under the command of Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were placed under whose command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know directly under whose command they were. All I know is of a man who arrested me, that he led a unit which was under the command of the accused, Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll address this a little later on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did the operation unit in this location start?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I think those operations started at around the 10th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you shelled?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Bjelasnica, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Which military formation shelled Bjelasnica?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: No, I think they were the units of the Army of Republika Srpska, under the direct command of Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please have the document bearing 65 ter number 7028 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, can you mark in this map where Bjelasnica - I'm sorry for the spelling - is?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you can't see Bjelasnica on this map, but it is located somewhere further down here. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you involved in the Defence of the village, and how?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor is leading the witness here and suggesting the answers, if Bjelasnica was a village. Bjelasnica is the highest mountain in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bjelasnica isn't a village. There's no larger mountain in Bosnia than Bjelasnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it is a mistake. I said "in the defence of any village," not "this village, Bjelasnica."

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: It's not a village. I directly took part at Igman, and I'm going to mark that in here. [Marks]. It's called Golo Brdo, directly above Ilidza, and I've drawn a circle, so that's the area, the general area, and I went there after the 16th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you explain what's Golo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: A plateau or, rather, a hill above Ilidza, within Mountain Igman, which is above Ilidza and above Hadzici. Ilidza is down there. [Marks]. Hadzici is further down, this way, to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So what did you mark in the map with a circle, exactly?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The place at which I was captured, Golo Brdo, above Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How was the defence in Golo Brdo organised?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many soldiers were involved in the defence of this area?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Twenty-five of us soldiers, members of the BH Army of the 101st Motorised Brigade, of which twenty-three were armed with just ten or fifteen bullets, and the rest didn't have any weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you describe how the battle unfolded?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, 1993, after noon, or maybe it was noon, there was heavy shelling that started, and it went on for about an hour or two hours. You lose a sense of time during moments like that, and that shelling went on for almost two hours. We were all in bunkers, and the bunkers were facing Bjelasnica and the Igman road.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What's happening later?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: After the shelling, when there was a lull, seven of us had to flee because the bunkers had been all but destroyed, so we had to take shelter in the next bunker or, rather, in the next two bunkers; or we had to move to a third bunker, in actual fact, so that when the shelling stopped, seven of us returned to our positions to pick up the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened later?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Since we, who were in the bunkers, and there were nine bunkers in all, I think, on Golo Brdo, we didn't have an overview of the positions, so we couldn't follow what was going on. We didn't have a view from Ilidza and Hadzici. And what happened was, quite simply -- well, I can now speak about myself and the other people who were captured by the Chetnik unit of Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many soldiers captured you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The Chetnik unit of Brne Gavrilovic, well, there were four, and the Army of Republika Srpska took three.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Each of those soldiers had more weapons than all of us put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What did you do when you understood that you had been captured?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The man who captured me, Pajkovic, took me to the next bunker, where three of my fellow -- fellows from my unit were already standing, their hands bound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have said that you were captured. Four people seemingly belonged to Gavrilovic's unit and three who were from the Republika Srpska. How were you able to make a difference and distinguish one from the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you understood. Four of us members of the BH Army were captured by a Chetnik unit. The other three were captured by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So four men from your unit were captured by the Chetniks, and three other men were captured by the Republika Srpska. Now it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How were the soldiers who captured you dressed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat, Mr. Ferrara. I don't think he heard your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How were the soldiers who captured you dressed, these members of this Chetnik unit?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Members of Brne's unit were all dressed in camouflage uniforms, black camouflage uniforms, and most of them had beards, whereas the Army of Republika Srpska, except for the commander, and I would learn later that he was commander of the -- former commander of the police, anyway, all but the commander wore the uniforms of the Army of Republika Srpska with the Serbian emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did they wear any particular patch or insignia?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Those emblems that I noticed when they were taking us to Brne were skulls with bones crossed, black.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please open the document bearing the 65 ter number 7222, page 79. Page 79, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, do you recognise this patch?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but what's written on them, I really couldn't make out, because in those moments I couldn't think of reading anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is saying, "Do you recognise this patch?" This is not a patch. This is a flag, and on this flag, the only thing is -- that the witness recognises, obviously, is the skull and bones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, we may have a problem. A flag is a flag, and a badge or an insignia is a badge or insignia. Could you ask the witness to specify what did he see exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, can you specify what did you see exactly in the uniform dressed by this Chetnik unit who captured you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: This is not an emblem that everybody had. Some had the sign of a skull with bones crossed over it, over the skull, whereas a couple of them had cockades on black caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please display, on the same 65 ter number, page 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Is this the cap are you talking about, or like this, of course?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Two or three of them had caps exactly like this, with these cockades. Whether the cockade is exactly identical, I'm not going to go into that. I was not able to observe details of that kind at that moment, but that's it, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did this kind of cap dressed by the Chetnik unit who captured you or by the other soldiers who captured your other -- your fellow men?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. There was no discussion about this cap. The only thing the witness recognised is the cap -- in fact the cockade with the traditional Serbian coat of arms. This is a Serbian traditional peasant's cap. It's green, as you can see on this photograph. The Prosecutor should not manipulate these photographs he's showing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, ask the witness to specify what he saw exactly, and amongst other things, the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutor did not manipulate anything, because the witness said at page 29, line 19, "Two or three of them had caps exactly like that." So maybe the accused should be more accurate when he makes his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So two or three of the Chetniks --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I listened carefully. The witness recognised the emblem. He didn't even mention the cap. I don't know what's in your transcript. I know what's heard in the courtroom. The witness did not mention this cap. He only recognised the emblem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I understood it to be the other way around. Maybe we have a problem with the interpretation. From what I understood, two had the same cap, but as far as the insignia is concerned, he can't say anything very precisely. I think the best would be for the witness to say exactly what he recognised, because it seems that Mr. Seselj has understood something else. So please tell us again, what did you see when you were arrested by these fighters? What were they wearing on their heads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat. Two or three men wore these traditional peasant caps with cockades. One of them had a larger black cap, also with a cockade, and the others who wore any emblems, some wore a skull with bones crossed beneath the skull, the others had signs of the skull with bones crossed on top of it, but what was written around these emblems I really couldn't read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you mentioned two things in your answer. You talk about the caps and you talk about the insignia on the clothing. These are two different things. What we are interested in, for the time being, is to understand what they were wearing on their heads. That is what we are interested in right now. Did they have insignia on their caps or what were they wearing on their heads? And if they were wearing insignia, what kind of insignia were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat. Two or three out of that unit that captured me wore these traditional peasant caps with cockades. I cannot remember the details of the cockades, but two or the three members of the Brne's unit wore these caps, so this kind of cap, with these cockades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What was the colour of these caps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell precisely, but they were not black. I cannot be more precise. I know they were traditional peasant caps. I know what they look like, with cockades in them. I cannot be precise about the colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, on the same document can we have on the screen page 83.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, do you recognise this patch?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes. But as to the writing around the skull and bones, I couldn't make it out. I couldn't see it well enough, because I told you some wore this kind of sign of skull and bones, the skull and bones behind the -- the bones behind the skull, and in other emblems the bones were under or above the skull.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what we have on our screen, the feeling I have is that this is an insignia which you stick on the arm, on the sleeve, or on the jacket, but this is perhaps placed on the hat or the cap. This insignia, which you recognise, where was it; on the jacket or was it on the cap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the uniforms of Brne's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the uniforms. Mr. Ferrara, I think you need to be very concise. You cannot make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Why do you continue to say that these men were a member of the Brne unit?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Because it was a Chetnik unit of vojvoda, the duke, Branislav Gavrilovic, known as Brne.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How did you come to know that they were a member of the Brne unit?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: When the three of us were brought by them to Brne at the foot of Golo Brdo hill, and when one of his men introduced him as a Chetnik vojvoda, Branislav Gavrilovic, known as Brne, the man whom we in Sarajevo had thought, quote/unquote, to be dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say that "three of us were brought by them to Brne," and you say, "at the foot of Golo Brdo hill." Mr. Registrar, can we please have -- Who did escort during -- from Golo Brdo to Brne camp?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: His men, his soldiers if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know the name or the nickname of this man?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I know of Pajkovic, the one who wanted to slit my throat. I know one name by the nickname of Major. I know one man's nickname was Copo, and another who came to prison to harass me, mistreat me, maltreat me, and the others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please have page 93 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, could you please take a look at this photograph. Were the men who escorted you dressed in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of them had caps and they were better armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender the document -- this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, could you please look at me. You are saying they were not wearing hats and they had better weapons. On this picture here, I hardly see any weapons. The flag-bearer doesn't seem to have a weapon; at least it's not apparent. The other one behind him with a beard might have a rifle across his back or something, but you can't see it. As for number 3 and 4, you can't see anything. So why are you saying that they had better weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just that the people -- the men who were leading us towards Branislav Gavrilovic were armed that way. I told you I had seen two or three of them with those caps with cockades, but as I said earlier, each one of them alone had more weapons than the seven of us put together.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, before he tenders this photograph into evidence, the Prosecutor must identify it. He must tell us what it means, who is on it, when it was taken and where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, where does this photograph come from? When was it taken? We see four guys with a flag in camouflaged dress, but that's all we see. So where does this photograph come from? Other than that, it's black and white, it's not a colour photograph. It might be a colour photograph, but you can't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course I'm not able to answer immediately, but after the break, I'm sure that I give you all the information you need. And the reason why I would like to tender this document is regarding the insignia and the patch and the flags and hat that the witness recognised; not, of course, the men displayed in the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Prosecutor, are we shown anything new that we have not already seen in the previous exhibits, and if that is so, can you tell us what new appears on this photo and why it is relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The witness said that it was exactly the cap and the patch dressed by the unit of Gavrilovic. Brne Gavrilovic is one of the Seselj vojvodas, so I think it's new information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This is completely untrue. The witness saw the caps, and the fur hat, called "subara," I suppose he didn't remember the exact name, but it's also a traditional Chetnik fur-lined hat. Here the people in the photograph are wearing completely different sort of caps. One of them is wearing a ski cap and the other one something entirely different. Please don't allow this to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will not admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we continue or it's time to have the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can continue for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, you say that there were other members of your unit that were captured. Can you tell us their names, please?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Krajisnik, Robert Kahrimanovic, and Rusmir -- the fourth was Rusmir. Myself, Rusmir, Robert and Zivko Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How did the soldiers who captured you treat you and the other three captives?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Robert was killed straight away at Golo Brdo, whereas I, Zivko Krajisnik and Rusmir were taken to Brne, because as far as I was able to hear, Brne had ordered us to be brought to him alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us how Robert was killed and who killed him?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I learned that later, that they had taken -- that they went to Brne, they had no losses, and Brne ordered all four to be brought to him. And that's when he started cursing our balijas mothers, that all of us should be killed immediately, that they must not take us down there alive. And then from that mass, I could distinguish only a barrel with a rifle grenade, and then that person who was shouting that they should kill us all, and then it all started flying at us. It must have been the Major who said he had to take us alive, and then a gunshot was heard that hit Robert in the back, whereas the Major just issued the order, "Disarm this sleaze bag, the one who is shooting."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did this happen before you were brought to Brne camp?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: No, Brne did not take part in that action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll break now. Mr. Ferrara, one small detail, please. The Registrar made some research and said that the photograph that we turned down and did not admit was already admitted through another witness. I don't really know under what conditions because I don't have this, but it has the number P455, which means, you know, that when the Prosecution is asking for documents to be tendered, we would like the Prosecution to make sure that it hasn't been done already. But we will now break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Seselj, at the beginning of this hearing you wanted to know whether last week, 35 minutes of your time hadn't been deducted from what was earmarked for your cross-examination. The Registrar gave us the detail for VS-1011. We have the time used for this witness by you. There's five pages of it. So if you remember, we were here at 8.30. The hearing started a bit late, and it started late, as I said, because of problems that had to do with your transfer. According to the documents I have here, we started at 9.17 a.m. The Registrar, regarding the cross-examination, made the countdown of the hours and minutes used, and according to the Registrar's log, you used two hours and one minute, and two hours had been given to you. Between 11.01 a.m. and 11.20, 17 minutes were used following an objection raised by the Prosecution about a document that you were going to use with one of your witnesses to come. The Trial Chamber said at that moment that the time spent was to be on you, but since that day the Trial Chamber was not pressed for time, we said that you could be allowed to use the 19 minutes to continue your cross-examination. The hearing ended at 1.05 p.m. It was scheduled to end at 1.15. But let me remind you that everyone was here at 8.30, and I was there at 8.20, actually. And the interpreters were here even earlier, some of them arrived even before me. We were not able to continue with the hearing, but when reading these documents, and of course your associates can take a look at them, during the cross-examination you used up two hours and one minute. So you cannot say that 35 minutes was deducted from your time. This is wrong. The Registrar will hand you this document. I will ask him to print out the five pages, and you will see exactly what happened, second after second. We now have the documents which tell us exactly when someone took the floor and when they stopped talking. In this document, there is a difference made between administrative procedures, the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination, procedure questions, and questions from the Bench. Everything is detailed in this document, and when reading it, you will see that you used up two hours. Now, Mr. Ferrara, you may resume. Mr. Seselj first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still insist that I used up only one hour and 25 minutes. After all, the entire examination of this last witness, apart from one or two minutes in closed session, is on my internet site, so whoever wishes to check this can with an ordinary stopwatch. You can do the math as to how long I actually examined the witness, effectively. I personally was stunned when you told me that my time was up, and my associates supported me because they measured the time very specifically. I don't know what criteria the Registry uses for measuring time. This doesn't say anything to me, but it is the recording that can be measured; that is to say, my questions to the witnesses and the witnesses' answers. My addressing the Trial Chamber cannot be incorporated, and also when there is a discussion between the Defence and the Prosecution. For me, this, what you gave me, is not an exact document, because I don't have your calculations in terms of the effective time before me. But everyone can see that on my internet site, and everyone can do the arithmetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are asking the Trial Chamber to go to your web site, the official -- your official site, but my official site is the Registrar's chart, and on this chart I know exactly when you took the floor, when you stopped talking, and so on, and it all adds up to two hours and one minute. That's all I can say. What else could I say? As an example, you took the floor for six minutes between 10.03 and 10.09, the same for -- there must have been an objection there, because you took the floor again from 10.14 to 10.20. So it's there. You know, you can monitor it second by second. Then the machine adds everything automatically and we end up with two hours and one minute. I'm not saying that there might not have been mistakes, mistakes are possible, but when I look at this chart, and as I told you over and over again, I'm always asking the Registrar to give me how much time you have left, and the Registrar hands me a document and says that this is the time left, and I tell you about it as quickly as possible. And when the Prosecution is asking the same question, I do the same thing so that everybody can know in realtime exactly what is happening. That's all. This is exactly what happened. Now, maybe your associates, if they were following on the internet, whenever we move into private session, maybe this is where they lose track of time, because since we're in private session, they can't follow. Check this closely. If need be, write submissions, and if it turns out that you're right - as things stand, I can't see how you could be - but if you are right, you will be given the time that you say you're missing for another witness. I'm not cutting time, you know, with scissors or something. We have time pressures and constraints, and we have to abide by that. Mr. Ferrara, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, before speaking of the killing of Robert, let's move back when you were captured. You say that you were captured by Brne men. You discovered later they were Brne men. Do you know what the specific task or role of this military formation during this battle was?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I cannot give a specific answer to that, but I know that Brne's unit was an independent one in this operation of taking Golo Brdo, because when Brne was taking me to the military police and when he handed me over to them, quite simply, the Military Police of Republika Srpska and the soldiers and all of them down there to whom he handed me over to -- let me use the Bosnian expression. I was terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know how did this military formation interact with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: No. As far as I could see, when Brne was handing me over to the military police, he said, quite simply, that I should not be harmed at all and that none of the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska should dare lay a hand on me, while the others quite simply accepted that as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the killing of Robert. Can you describe again, because I checked the transcript and it's not very clear, how did it happen? Where you were exactly -- where were you, exactly?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: There was this small depression there. Golo Brdo is called that, "the naked hill," because it is pure rock and nothing else. When Pajkovic threw me there, on my left was Robert, and I really cannot remember who was on my right. I fell somehow as Pajkovic threw me there next to Robert. At any rate, Robert was on my left-hand side, and at the moment when the Major talked to someone, using a Walkie-Talkie or some kind of radio communication equipment, I just heard him say, "There are no losses," and also that the boss is supposed to take all four of us, but alive. That is when this commotion took place. In this commotion, I just heard someone hollering that we should all be killed, and this person was swearing at us, cursing our balija mothers, that Serbs were being killed in Sarajevo and they want to take us alive. I just saw that rifle then, but I don't know who fired it. After the gunshot, the Major said that that person, that trash, as he said, should be disarmed. I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Registrar is mentioning a mistake. Line 2, page 41, on line 3 it says "I was terrified," or it says "He was terrified," so maybe you need to ask the witness who was terrified, whether it was him who was terrified or someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who was terrified by Brne?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: At that point in time, we didn't know -- or, rather, I didn't know about Brne, so of course I was terrified, because Pajkovic had promised to slit my throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Is it correct, "I was terrified"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So how old was Robert at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I think he was just 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could you see the perpetrator from your position?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Why? How were you positioned?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: All four of us were lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Was Robert maltreated before he was killed, beaten, or questioned in some way?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I don't know. When Pajkovic brought me to those three men, Robert was still alive. In the meantime, when I fell down between Robert and I don't know who was to my right, whether Krajisnik or Rusmir, I'm not sure, the Major informed us that they -- they said that they had had no losses, and that's when he received an order, I suppose, to take all four of us alive to the chief, I think he said, or the boss. And this resulted in a reaction, a revolt. I can't say what I didn't see, but after the shooting and when it became clear to them that Robert was dead, the Major ordered the disarming -- that the person who did the shooting should be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who was in charge of this group?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The Major at Golo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened after the killing of Robert?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: They tied up our hands of all three of us on our backs, and in a column we went down Igman for about 20 minutes, until we reached a clearing of Golo Brdo. And when we reached the clearing, they ordered us to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who was in charge during the escort?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Behind me was Pajkovic, and he was hitting me with his rifle-butt and with his hand on my head, until Copo told him not to hit me or the others. Actually, behind me was Rusmir and in front Zivko, but the Army of Republika Srpska -- I mean, the soldiers who were passing by - I couldn't see behind me, I could see them next to me - but every soldier in an SMB uniform who would try to walk up to us or to hit us would get a response by way of swearing, "Go to Golo Brdo, catch yourself some balijas. These are ours," meaning, "our prisoners," their prisoners, because they had taken us prisoner. So until we got down there to that clearing, none of these people who were climbing up Golo Brdo in uniform didn't dare lay a hand on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What does it mean, "balija"? Can you explain to us?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: It's a Serb derogatory term for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please have again the document bearing 65 ter number 7028 on the screen. It's the map that we already showed to the witness, with the marks, the one with the marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, could you please mark in the map the location where you were taken to after you were captured?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: This is too small. I will try, roughly. [Marks]. It's roughly around here, although this is too small a map. So it's from here [indicates], Golo Brdo, where I marked it, above Ilidza, towards Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Is this location you marked in blue the Brne camp?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: This is where Brne was waiting, was waiting for them to bring the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, when we subsequently bring this map up again, we will have no idea of what it is. So before you save it, I would suggest you ask the witness to indicate, by numbers or by some other means, what the points on the map are, because otherwise we'll just see a red circle and a blue cross and we'll have no idea what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, can you -- in the circle, you said before it was Golo Brdo. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you put an "A" near the circle?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: [Marks] This is Golo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where there is now the blue mark, the blue mark you said was where Brne was waiting, can you put a "B" near that mark?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: [Marks] This is the place where Brne was waiting for them to bring us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number P460.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How were you treated during the transfer to Mountain Igman, where Brne was waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. You cannot put questions this way, "How were you treated during the transfer to Mount Igman, where Brne was waiting for you?" He was taken prisoner at Igman, and now he is descending from Igman. The Prosecutor should really focus on the subject of this testimony. How can he put this kind of question, "How were you treated during the transfer to Mount Igman, where Brne was waiting for you?" I mean, this is so absurd. It cannot be any more absurd than this. They took them down Igman, where Brne was waiting for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, when coming down Mount Igman, at what point was the witness ill-treated? Was it when he descended Mount Igman or when he got there? Please put your questions in such a way that we know exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How were you treated during the transfer to Brne, where Brne was waiting for you, from Golo Brdo to where Brne was waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: From Golo Brdo to where Brne was waiting for us, I will repeat, Pajkovic beat me until Copo warned him not to touch me anymore. When they brought us to Brne, when we sat down, three or four times -- of course, I didn't feel the pain then. Three or four times, someone hit me from the back on the head until Brne signaled with his eyes, and then that person stopped hitting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the destination, who was present?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: We were ordered to sit down on the ground, so that's what we did. Copo, Pajkovic and the Major made a circle around us. We were sitting down there, and Copo and the Major and Pajkovic went some 20 metres further away and returned several minutes later with a tall man wearing black, clean-shaven, hair cut short, and then the Major said, "This is Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, a Chetnik vojvoda."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Had you ever seen or meet Brne before?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I had heard of him and I might have seen him one or two times while he was working, and I think he worked at Bascarsija, in the Hamam bar, but I was never introduced to him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many individuals were there in total? You say Brne, Pajkovic, Copo, Major. Were there any other people?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: In the circle around us, of course, I didn't count them, but there were at least some 50 people in the circle around us who, in fact, didn't say one single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How were these people dressed?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, some wearing black uniforms, like the others, the other ones. I don't know how many there were in the unit, but they were all armed to the teeth with hand grenades, pistols, automatic rifles, knives. Each of Brne's men had a number of weapons, more weapons than, well, half our unit, if I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened when you were there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: They started interrogating us in complete silence. Brne asked the questions. First he asked Rusmir, then Zivko. Then he asked me, and then he went back to Rusmir. Afterwards, he went on to Zivko again. Well, I don't know how long that went on for, but at one point when Brne asked Zivko Krajisnik who -- what Momo Krajisnik was to him, this one answered that it was a relative of his. And then the next question was, "Are you a Serb," and Krajisnik said, "Yes, I am." And then Brne kicked him with his right leg -- foot in his head, and he fell into my lap. And I was ordered to lift him up, to make him sit up straight, and then the next question came, and that was, "Are you a Serb?" And once again the answer was, "Yes, I am," and another blow. And I think that Zivko was already half -- well, semi-conscious. Then he asked him, "Do you think Momo is going to help you out now?" And Zivko made a sign with his head. Then Brne swore and cursed Krajisnik, Mladic, Karadzic and so on, cursing their mothers, and said that Seselj was the be-all and end-all in Sarajevo, God and the law, and that Karadzic or Mladic or Krajisnik would not be able to help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened to Zivko Krajisnik and Rusmir later on?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
