utterances.text: Nobody touched Rusmir, because as Brne said, he's with his people, but what Zivko -- he asked us what Zivko and I were doing in the army, although we claimed at the time that we had been mobilised. He crouched down next to Zivko and did this with his fingers [indicates]. He began breaking his nose, the cartilage of his nose, with his fingers, and he said, "Repeat that again. Say you're a Serb again and I'll rip your head off."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened later?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I don't know, but Copo, Pajkovic, the Major and Brne went some five or six metres away from us and they talked about something. I don't know what. Brne returned and pointed a pistol to Krajisnik and said, "Kill the Ustasha and you're free, get out of my sight. If you want to go back to Sarajevo, go. If you want to stay with the Serbs, stay. I'm not interested in that, but kill the Ustasha and you're free," handing him a pistol. Krajisnik took the pistol, but he did not -- well, I don't think he even realised he was holding a pistol in his hand. He held it at the level of my face, and I moved my head at one point to avoid Pajkovic's knife, thinking that if there was a bullet, at least the bullet would save me from the knife. Brne, I assume, noticed that, and he started shouting at Krajisnik. He swore at him and cursed his Serbian mother, and then he told him to shoot me. He repeated that. Krajisnik did not shoot. Then Brne seized the pistol out of his hand, handed it to me. I took the pistol, pointed it at Krajisnik, and that same second Brne got hold of my wrist and took the pistol away from me. The pistol, of course, was empty. He said to me that not a hair on my head would be harmed, and his own men, he said that had he had ten men like that, he wouldn't look at Sarajevo from Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: After this part, you're absolute, what happened? What happened after this particular act, the one that Brne said, "If I had ten such men with me, I wouldn't be watching Sarajevo from the Trebevic Mountain"?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: He ordered -- well, for Krajisnik directly, not for Rusmir, but for Krajisnik he ordered, "Take him away." That was the order. He said, "Take him away. Take the trash away. Kill the trash." That kind of thing. And then Copo took Krajisnik aside and fired a whole clip from the automatic rifle at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you see Copo shooting at Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes. It was just a few metres away from where I was and where Brne was, three or four metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened to Rusmir?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I did not see them take Rusmir away. However, afterwards, when we set out towards the police administration in Blazuj, from the bushes I saw legs protruding and assumed that that was Rusmir. And the next day, when Pajkovic came to see me and bring me some cigarettes, he said he had killed him and that that was the first time that Brne took someone off his knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know why were you saved by Brne?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably because of the fact that I had taken the pistol that he handed to me and because throughout the questioning I looked him in the eyes. He could have done it the next day, when they found my BH Army identity card, because Copo arrived, and Pajkovic with him, and they even said that -- well, I don't want to say ugly words here, but they said that I was brazen enough to lie him in the eyes and that that helped save my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you identify the body of Rusmir later on?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes. In 1994, in mid-June, I think, 1994, after my escape from the camp and when the investigation was completed in Sarajevo, together with his wife and Amor Masovic, we carried out the identification of Rusmir's body. But Zivko Krajisnik, well, we never managed to identify him because his family members in -- he didn't have any family members in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How did you identify the body of Rusmir; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: During the questioning in front of Brne up there, Rusmir and Zivko had to take off their camouflage uniforms. And as he was taking off his camouflage uniform, Rusmir took off -- I saw his pants, his underpants. Well, actually, they were swimming trunks, in which he was later exchanged dead. And his wife, with his mother -- together with his mother, helped identify him by some injuries he had sustained previously which were evident on the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened after the killing of Krajisnik and Rusmir? Where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Copo and Brne, in a Golf car, drove us down Igman where there's a turning in Blazuj, where there were three or four trucks. His unit went off in trucks, whereas the three of us got into a white Golf car, and Brne drove me to the military police. When we entered the premises, I knew some people there who were from Ilidza. Brne asked that we be brought some coffee and ordered them -- and told them that they weren't to touch me. And then he learnt, and that's when I learnt this, too, that three more men had been captured, but I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you recognise someone in particular in Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The people that I recognised in Blazuj were members of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Military Police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How did these people treat Brne?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Servants.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What did Brne do and what did he say at the compound to these people, when they were delivered there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Well, they said something along the lines that he didn't have any losses at Golo Brdo. He said that we should be brought some coffee and that we could smoke a cigarette, and he wanted to see the other three men who had been captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am listening very carefully to what you are saying and how you are describing these events. There are some questions that come automatically to mind. You said that you descended Mount Igman and you reached Blazuj, where the Military Police of the Republika Srpska took charge. In the Golf there are three of you, Brne, you and your comrade. In the Golf, were you tied up, were you handcuffed? How were you sitting in the car, in the Golf car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the interpretation was. After the killing of Zivko Krajisnik and Rusmir, we went down to the parking lot, where the trucks were, and Brne, myself and Copo, Brne's man, got into a Golf car. Brne drove me, together with Copo, to the military police, to Blazuj. So they weren't my co-fighters. It was Brne and his man Copo who took me in a white Golf car. They drove me to Blazuj and handed me over there to the Military Police of Republika Srpska. So they weren't any fellow combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I've understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Brne had a conversation with anyone at Blazuj regarding yourself?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: All he said was why did he spare me, and wanted to see the other three men after we had had our coffee. He asked to see the other three men who had been captured. I didn't know who else had been captured of my fellow fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you questioned in Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Not in front of Brne. Let me repeat, Brne wanted to see the other three men who had been captured, so when they took me off to the room, which was a makeshift prison, actually, Hilmija Numic was there, Dragan Despotovic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What did Brne say to these men?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Hasib -- the other man's name was Hasib. I can't remember his surname. But, anyway, when they took me inside, Brne asked for the names, and he said to Hasib and Hilmija that with their own people -- that they were with their own people, and he said to Dragan Despotovic that he should thank God for the fact that the military police had captured him and not him, himself, that he hadn't captured him. Later on, in the seven months that followed that I spent as a camp inmate, as a detainee, I learnt -- well, I don't know if it's true or not, but this is what I heard, that in order to avoid being mistreated, it was enough for me to say that I was Brne's prisoner and that nobody would dare touch me then. And he said that to Dragan, because Dragan Despotovic was a Serb, himself. And everything -- everybody who was in the BH Army who wasn't a Muslim was not worthy of living at all. And while Brne was there, he did not touch any of those three other men, my co-fighters. There was no interrogation while he was there. The interrogation started when he left, after he had left the compound of that military police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you recall if Brne talked to you before leaving?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: He repeated that not a hair of my head was to be harmed, and he said that to the soldiers, too, the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska who were nearby. As for the other three men, he said he wasn't interested in what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you ever see Brne again?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: He came the next day, when they found my military ID papers. He came with Copo and brought a shirt and some cigarettes, and asked -- he said that his men would come in in the following days as well to ask whether anybody had dared touch me, and what he would say to the people. And for seven days and six nights, every -- we were subjected every second to beatings and intimidation. We were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who perpetrated these beatings?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: The members of the Army of Republika Srpska, the interrogators.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did the Brne men come to visit you in the following days?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever -- well, they would come for three or four days after that, and whenever they came, at least Copo and Pajkovic, they would bring a couple of boxes of cigarettes, and they said that Brne had sent them, except for that smaller one, Goran, who would come alone, probably without Brne's knowledge, and he would mistreat me, especially me. He would put a hand grenade between my legs. He would intimidate me in various ways and hoped that he had instilled fear into me. He wanted to make me afraid. I thought that that was -- I think that that was on day 5. Actually, he stopped coming on day 5, I think. Now, whether any of the soldiers -- or perhaps this man Dragan Mircic, who was the commander, might have said to Copo or Pajkovic that Goran was coming specially to see me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Was this Goran a member --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Prosecutor. I'm watching the clock. Today, we started late, so maybe we could have only one break, but we have a problem with the tape. That would mean we would have to stop and break by 20 to 7.00, so there are two possibilities. Either we continue without any break, and we will stop at a quarter to 7.00, or we have a break now and resume after 20 minutes. I believe that you have 50 to 55 minutes left, but I'm sure Mr. Registrar will tell me exactly how much time you still have. The best would be to finish the examination-in-chief today. How do you want us to proceed? Would you rather that we have a break now or that we continue until the bitter end? A break? Mr. Mundis asked for a break, so we will have a 15-minute break and we will resume at 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Let me tell the Prosecutor that the Registrar told me you had 44 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Koblar, I was asking you, was this Goran a member of the Brne unit?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did he force to you to do something in particular or do you remember something?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Goran was the only one among them who forced us to sing Chetnik songs, to pray to Allah, to bend on our knees -- to go down on our knees. I'm talking about Brne's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many days were you detained in Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Six days and six nights, and on the seventh day we had to relocate from Blazuj to Kula because the local inhabitants of Hadzici wanted to come for us; to lynch us, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where were you transported from Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: What is now Kula Prison used to be a wartime prison, and it was used for members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially Muslims, at least those who reached Kula alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How long were you detained in Kula?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: For us, Kula was just a basis, a place where we were registered by the International Red Cross, but we spent all our time doing labour around Sarajevo, digging trenches, going ahead of the defence lines to do some repair in case of attacks, and that would be usually from 6.00 a.m. going on as late as midnight. Sometimes -- I was in Kula until the 17th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please see the documents -- the document 65 ter number 7233 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes. That's the official certificate from the International Red Cross, that I'm recorded under the number stated here as a war prisoner in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When was it signed?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: This document I asked to get subsequently, but I was registered on the 3rd of August, 1993, as you see in the document. And it says in the document -- I mean, the date when I escaped from Kula is also recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number P461.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What were your conditions in Kula; how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I came here to tell the truth. There were no problems in Kula. We were not mistreated, except some individuals. But also I have to say that the commander at Kula and his deputy, as well as those who designated working groups, labour groups, never asked themselves how we were treated by Serb soldiers at labour sites where we went. They didn't care whether anyone would get killed, whether somebody would stray into a minefield, whether anyone would be beaten up or wounded. We were just slaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What were these labour groups you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Wherever work force was needed to dig trenches, communicating trenches, and even some private work for individuals, we were sent to do it. The only place where I was in those seven months was in Trebevic, at Radomir Kojic's place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you recall the locations where were you forced -- where were you brought to do this kind of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: From Hrasnica, the Famos factory, Lukavica, Dobrinja 1 and 4, Pale, Mount Trebevic, Crepoljsko, Spicasta Stijena. I cannot remember anymore, but essentially anywhere where something needed to be done for the Serb army, we had to do it, even if it was on the frontline itself or sometimes behind the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Witness, I see this certificate of the International Committee of the Red Cross, that you had visits from time to time. I would like to know about the staff of the Red Cross. I'd like to know whether the staff of the Red Cross actually questioned you and obtained information on forced labour and on the conditions under which you were forced to do this labour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they visited once a month to bring us toiletries. They would distribute a pack or two of cigarettes to everyone, and they brought some food for a proper meal that we never got in Kula, but we never received it, actually. It was used by others. It was pocketed by the Serb Army. However, the Red Cross was helpless to change anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was the following: I wanted to know whether they questioned you on what you were doing, what you had to do. Did you tell the International Red Cross that you were forced to do labour, and did you tell them about the conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: One of the locations that you mentioned was Spicasta Stijena. Do you remember a man called Vaso Baricanin when you were there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes. It's a member of the Army of Republika Srpska who introduced himself as a Chetnik, and I'll certainly never forget him as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Why you never forget him?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: When he found out that we were members of the BH Army and that I was captured by Brne's Chetniks, he made very nasty pranks every day, like throwing dynamite into my trench, shooting right next to my head or ears, throwing grenades next to the spot I was working at, and he even made me dig my own grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: At some time during this period, did you get hill?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: After one BH Army attack, we were going out to Spicasta Stijena. One bunker was damaged so with two other men, other inmates, I had to go outside the bunker to repair the damage caused by the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you ever used as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Not literally, but it was quite enough to be forced to go between two lines of fire and do some silly work that didn't even need to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you forced to do working on a minefield?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: At the Famos factory in Hrasnica, Mandic, whose first name I can't recall now, forced me to go between two lines of fire and cut the grass, the dry grass that didn't bother anyone because it was the month of September.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: December, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: So I almost came up to the bunker where there were members of the BH Army, and from that point I retraced my steps back, following my own footprints in the snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You said, and it is confirmed by the document we tendered -- we already tendered, your detention in Kula lasted until 17 February 1994. How did you manage to escape from Kula?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I had been preparing my escape ever since I started working at that farm, because that was the only place from which it was safe to attempt to escape without risking the lives of others who were working with me, who might be killed, because I was always told -- warned, in fact, that in case anyone attempts to escape, everybody in that group would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, why is it that you were so sure that the people working in the same group as you would not be killed? How were you so sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that farm, in the second shift there were only two men, Velija Tiro and I. Velija was supposed to escape with me, but to protect his father, who stayed at Kula, he changed his mind. And the guard who led us there that night was a man who never laid a finger on us, so I was sure that when they'd discover I'd escaped, that guard would not allow anything to happen to Velija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please have on the screen the document bearing 65 ter number 7237.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, can you comment on this document? What does it show?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: This is a certificate from the state commission searching for missing persons, signed by its chairman at the time, Mr. Amor Masovic. It confirms my capture and my detention in the camp from the 17th of July, 1993, to 17 February 1994, and it is attested by a stamp, the stamp that the accused also challenges.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, objection. On this document, we read "Bosnia-Herzegovina, State Commission Searching for Missing Persons." The date is 13 April 1999. On the stamp, it also says "Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Justice and General Administration, State Commission Searching for Missing Persons, Sarajevo." This was four years after the Dayton Accords. This could not have been the official stamp of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It couldn't have been the state commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do not doubt the veracity of the details in the certificate, that this witness escaped from Kula without any help from the state commission, but this cannot be the stamp of the state commission of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina because that republic had completely different emblems at the time. These are emblems of the Muslim authorities. It can't even be the emblems of the Federation. The Federation is -- has the combination of the coat of arms of the -- something adopted by Muslims and another part is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... cross-examination. We are not listening, Mr. Seselj testifying on the stamps of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. An objection was raised. He's saying that this is a forged document, just when you're asking for this document to be tendered. Witness, you heard what Mr. Seselj said. The stamp that we have here, which comes from the Federation, well, according to Mr. Seselj, the coat of arm on this stamp is not the one that was used in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in 1999, since this document was drafted on April 13, 1999, there could not be this type of stamp. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat. I don't know when the High Commissioner adopted the new joint flag, the coat of arms and emblems of the federation for all cantons. This document is still filed in the building of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the same number, with the same commission. Now, why this stamp is here, I don't want to go into what the accused keeps repeating, that these are some kind of Serbian coat of arms. It's up to the Court and the Office of the Prosecutor. This, however, is an official document that is still filed in the building of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will consult with my fellow Judges to see whether we admit this document or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, after having deliberated, feels that there are sufficient indicia for liability, notwithstanding the presence of the stamp, holds that we shall admit this document. Can we have a number, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P462.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have one question I'd like to put to you, Witness. You've said that you escaped from the farm where you were doing forced labour. When you were working on this farm, guarded by someone, were you asked whether you wanted to go and work on the farm or did you have to go and work on the farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Going to work on the farm was something that only somebody who knew how to do agricultural labour -- who knew something about agriculture or who was ill. And before I went to the farm, on two occasions I had pneumonia and a perforation of my ulcer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to know is this: In the prison at Kula, did somebody come 'round and say, "Are there any volunteers to go and work in the fields? And those who are volunteers, stand out, and those people will go," or the guards at the prison in Kula said, "You, you and you, you shall leave and go on the farm"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of us had any choice. We couldn't choose where we would go to do labour, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my question. We have under half an hour left. Mr. Seselj, you can start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I always like not wasting time in vain, and if there's half an hour, I can deal with an area that I intend to cover and finish that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Koblar, your father is a Slovene; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And your mother is a Serb from Berane; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: She's not a Serb, she's a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Previously, you had said she was a Serb when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I never represented my mother as being a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. And Berane is a town in Montenegro; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I was born in Ivangrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's the town of Berane which during the communist period was called "Ivangrad" following the name of a top-ranking communist official, am I right? So it is the town of Berane, it's one and the same thing, and during the communist period it changed its name and took the name of Ivan Milutinovic and became Ivangrad, is that right, Ivan Milutinovic being a communist leader?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment on your position towards the former regime, but, yes, that is the same town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's not up to you to comment. Just answer my questions. You're not allowed to comment in that sense, just to answer my questions. You've just said that in the ethnic sense, you declared yourself as being a Yugoslav; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had in mind the fact that your parents were of different ethnicities, and there were many people like that in the former Yugoslavia, and usually they would declare themselves as Yugoslavs for that reason; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Neither my father nor my mother ever forced us to declare ourselves in any particular way. They left it to us. It was up to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you declared yourself as a Yugoslav because you were from a mixed marriage. There were many people like you who did the same; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there were any people who were not from mixed marriages, whose parents were of the same nationality or ethnicity, and would also declare themselves as being Yugoslav because they wanted to see a united, uniform Yugoslav state and they were loyal to that state? Were there people like that too?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you have declared yourself as being a Bosnian, ethnically speaking; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I said that that's everybody's private affair, how they choose to declare themselves, but my answer to your question is "yes".

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have to declare -- you have to answer private questions as well here, of a private nature. If something is an intimate question, then we can go into private session, if you think that something is offensive. But this isn't, because you said yourself that you declared yourself a Bosnian, your answer was "yes." Right. Now you know that there are many people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, more than a million, who declare themselves as Bosniaks, who declare their ethnicity as being Bosniak; right? Will you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you, who declare yourselves as being Bosnians, and those other people who declare themselves as being Bosniaks, is that the same nation, the same ethnic group, or are they two different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have to answer my question. I know that you don't like the question, but you have to answer it.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: There are Bosnians and Serbs and Muslims and Croats, and the fact that most people declare themselves as being Bosniaks, that's an ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you say there are Serbs, Croats and Muslims who declare themselves as Bosnians, then that's regional affiliation, territorial affiliation, and in that sense I'm a Bosnian, too, because I was born in Sarajevo, although I'm a Serb by ethnicity. Isn't that right, am I right in saying that? You lived in the same building in Sarajevo in which I lived before I moved to Belgrade. It's Obala, the 27th of July, number 61; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I lived on the sixth floor in the building, and the family of the man who moved into my flat when I left during the war was killed. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: That's directly the unit in which I was from the beginning of the war, and that particular unit never, ever killed a Serb or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What happened to the family who lived on the sixth floor of the building in the 27th of July Street, number 61, in the flat I lived in until 1986; what happened to that family?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I don't know what family you mean. I know all the neighbours from 1984. They're all alive and well except those who died of old age.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you know nothing about that family?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I don't know what family you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is the Bajic family on the sixth floor of that apartment building, and they had a two-room flat. What happened to them? You provided security for the building during the war, so what happened to them? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: While I was in Kula, most probably they were moved to Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All trace of them is lost, and they turn up on the list of missing persons who were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: All I can say is that I guarantee that from that particular address, as it's called now, Aleja Lipa 51, nobody lost their lives or were killed by members of the BH Army or my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How do you know that that didn't happen while you were a prisoner in detention during those seven months you told us about?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I don't know about that period of time, but I also do know full well that all the people from my unit -- I know all the people from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you confirm that whatever ethnicity for us born in Bosnia, according to regional affiliation, we're termed "Bosnians," but you said that you were a Bosnian by ethnicity; is that what you said? Right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: That's how I declare myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the Bosnian nation exists as well. In addition to those of us whose regional affiliation is declared as Bosnian, we were born there, but are of different ethnicities, there's a nation that calls itself "the Bosnian nation," so you are a member of that nation. And we concluded that the Bosniak nation exists as well. There's a large group of people, more than a million, in fact, who say of themselves that they are Bosniaks, and we have to recognise their right to declare themselves in that way, because everybody has the right to declare themselves in any way they like. Now, the Bosnians, by ethnicity, is it the same as the Bosniaks, by ethnicity, would you say, or are they two different ethnicities or two different nations? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Well, if the Serbs and Croats exist, and the Macedonians and Slovenians, why shouldn't the Bosnians exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not asking you why they don't exist. They do exist, because if you say you're a Bosnian, your nationality is Bosnian, that means they do exist, a group of people calling themselves "Bosnians." Now, my question to you is this: Are the Bosnians, nationality-wise, the same as the Bosniaks? Is their ethnicity and nationality the same, the Bosnians and Bosniaks? That's my question, but you seem to be avoiding answering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, this is an important question for the Trial Chamber. Please try and answer the question which is being put to you. The question is extremely clear. If you cannot answer the question, say so. But in light of your education, you are intellectually capable of telling us the difference between the Bosniak and Bosnian nation. You, yourself, refer to which nation, irrespective of everything that happened? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, the present situation is such in Bosnia that the Bosniaks are a nation, an ethnic group, whereas we Bosnians belong to the category of miscellaneous or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I've understood your answer correctly, the Bosniaks are one nation, recognised as such, whereas you Bosnians are not recognised as a separate nation or ethnic group because there are little of you, so you are listed under the column of "Other." Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you could have given me that answer straight away and not waste time. Now, you also told us that you testified while you were in detention. Does that mean that you gave a statement to the Serbian military authorities after you'd been captured?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes, when Brne handed me over to the military police in Blazuj the Military Police of the Army of Republika Srpska, conducted an investigation, but we did not sign any statements, any of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you said here that you testified within the frameworks of an investigation. When you testify within an investigation, you give some sort of statement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Let me repeat. The Military Police of Republika Srpska did not ask us to make any statement. All they asked was that we tell them about each other and the positions where our army unit's positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, why, when you were interviewed by the Military Police of Republika Srpska, did you never tell them that three of your fellow combatants, Rusmir Hamalukic -- you forgot his surname, but that's his surname, isn't it, Hamalukic? You see, I know his surname, you don't. Then the other man, Rusmir --

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Robert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, Robert Kahrimanovic and Zivko Krajisnik. Why did you not tell the Military Police of Republika Srpska that they had been captured first and killed second?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Dragan Micic, the commander of the police of Republika Srpska, I told him that Robert -- that we had been captured and that Robert Kahrimanovic, Rusmir and Zivko had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All you told him was that you had been captured, but that they were killed when your bunker was shelled?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: That's a sheer lie, blatant lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, if it's a lie. You said here also that your unit, your group numbering 50 men, was sent from Grbavica to Mount Bjelasnica for preparations and rest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what preparations could you have had on Mount Bjelasnica when you had taken part before that in fighting in town, in the town, and your intention was to fight for the town, who was going to take what settlement, who was going to defend which settlement and so on, so what preparations were you sent to -- from Grbavica, surrounded under Muslim control, that you went to a mountain, Mount Bjelasnica, outside of town? What kind of preparations were they, then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: It was planned that during that year, the deblocking of Sarajevo was to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what kind of rest was it if you went as reinforcements to the Muslim units who were already on Bjelasnica? Then it's not rest. You were sent as reinforcements to the units who wanted to lift the siege of the Muslim part of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Well, you know total national defence better than me, but don't forget that during that period, there was a war on between the Bosniaks and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's got nothing to do with this. The war between the Muslims and Croats broke out in other areas. You were sent from Sarajevo to reinforce the Muslim units on Bjelasnica; right? There's no other rational explanation, because if -- for somebody to send you to a war zone for you to have a rest, that's absurd. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: It wasn't Muslim units, it was the BH Army. Now, the fact that you call them that way --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Listen, you have to answer my questions. That army could have called itself what it wanted, the Cerkez army, for instance. It's name could have been any other, like the Martian army or whatever, but the vast majority of the people in that army were the Muslims, and they were fighting the Serb army, on the one side, and the Croatian Army on the other. And in the Serb army we had Muslims and Croats as well, and in the Croatian Army there were Muslims -- I haven't heard that there were any Serbs there, but it wouldn't surprise me if a Serb happened to find his way there, too. Anyway, answer the question. Did you go as reinforcements, your group of 50 soldiers, or not? Did you go as reinforcements or did you go to take a rest in the area of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Nobody was told -- none of us were told that we were going as reinforcements or had any combat assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I'll say I believe you for the time being. Anyway, you crossed over -- you ran across the runway at Sarajevo Airport to go to Bjelasnica; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Sarajevo Airport was under the control of the United Nations at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were not able to -- you couldn't have run across the runway without the UN observers seeing you; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: You would run across the runway between midnight and 4.00 or 5.00 a.m., in the period when there was the least frequency, UNPROFOR frequency there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's because you were afraid of the Serb snipers or artillery fire; that's why you had to run across the runway after midnight. However, the UN forces had the IC devices for night observation, they had night-sights, UNPROFOR; right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You couldn't have run across the Sarajevo runway without UN forces giving you permission to do that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you were digging the tunnel underneath the airport, do you mean to say that the UN forces did not know that you were busy digging a tunnel?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: I learned about the tunnel only sometime in October 1993, perhaps even November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It doesn't matter at all when you learned about the tunnel. In October or December 1993, you were in captivity. Maybe you found out while you were in captivity. That means the Serb found out about it too. Do you agree with me that it's impossible for the tunnel to have been dug under the Sarajevo airfield without the UN forces knowing anything about it?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: It's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: If you shut a mouse, he will find a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I agree you acted as mice when you were digging a hole, but that hole could not have been dug without the UN forces knowing, if the Serb forces knew and if they were trying to impede the digging of the tunnel by targeting the beginning and the end of the tunnel with artillery, is that correct; they did that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: We did run across, that's true. I don't know if you had occasion -- if you allow me, Your Honour, to ask a counter-question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. It is not your questions, but it is the witness [as interpreted] who's putting a question. If you know, answer the question, but if you don't know, don't answer the question. But please answer. He is entitled to ask you any question he likes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you this again. The tunnel was dug without the knowledge of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we could then draw the inference that all the soldiers of the UNPROFOR were cretins. If they were guarding the airport and the airfield and the runway while somebody was digging a tunnel underneath and the Muslim forces were going through the tunnel safely, transporting ammunition, weaponry and all the supplies, how come the UNPROFOR didn't know anything about it? What kind of imbeciles did they mobilise into their forces? The only possible conclusion is that the forces of the UNPROFOR knew about the tunnel and they allowed it to be dug.

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what is true?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: You are making inferences. I'm telling you it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You graduated from the School of Political Science at the university where I used to teach?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: You were a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're not well informed. I was a professor as well later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, is it your position that the UN would have been under an obligation to prevent the digging of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. UN troops were obliged -- were duty-bound to be neutral and to position themselves between the warring parties. They were securing the airport so that humanitarian aid could arrive, and they were duty-bound to prevent any misuse of the airport for war purposes. Instead, they made it possible for Muslim forces to dig the tunnel. I want to compromise the United Nations, because their forces provided combat cooperation to Muslim forces against Serb forces, and I have done this successfully. The United Nations have been compromised by me, because I am their enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we listened to your story at the airport. We could imagine you crossing the runway between midnight and 4.00 in the morning. This may sound surprising, since, normally speaking, the UN forces do use binoculars and night-sights, and they would probably see people running across the airport at that time. A second reason to be surprised, this tunnel under the airport, from what I understood, you said to begin with that you were in Kula and that you knew nothing about this, and in the various answers you provided, you then said that a tunnel was being built -- was being dug. Now, when did you hear about it? Was it after the war, when you were in Sarajevo, when you were at Kula? When did you hear about this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you were in prison in the camp at Kula; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an important question: When the tunnel was dug, according to you, was it the Muslim Army that dug this tunnel, with the agreement of the UN forces, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The BH Army alone, without anyone's cooperation or assistance, using the fighting men of the BH Army, and that is what I learned after I escaped from Kula and rejoined my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few minutes left. Since it is 18.57, one last question, Mr. Seselj, before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me then settle the issue of the airport so I don't have to come back to it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are aware, Mr. Koblar, that the airport, at the beginning of the war, was held by the Serb forces; right? Do you know that the United Nations, and Western powers, and Americans, and Brits, and the French, exerted pressure on Republika Srpska to cede control over the airport to the United Nations; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: That was a decision made by the International Community in view of all that happened during the war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Republika Srpska hand over the airport?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: In 1992, as far as I know, Republika Srpska did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. That's what the name was; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Yes, but it was never legally established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. Do you imagine I don't know what you would respond? I'm not asking you about your theoretical opinion. I'm asking you: Is it true that the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which did not exist, as you say, hand over the airport to the United Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA KOBLAR
utterances.text: Whether it did or didn't, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you don't know. The Judges do know, and the United Nations do know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we shall stop now. You may, if need be, continue on this topic tomorrow. For your associates in Belgrade who are keeping track of the time, it is 18.57 and 21 -- and 34 seconds. You have 21 minutes left -- you have had 21 minutes so far.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we shall resume again tomorrow at a quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
